worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: From a sound to a meaning
worked.scenario: You hear a brief tone and recognize it as a phone notification.
steps: The vibration is a stimulus. Hair cells in the inner ear are mechanoreceptors that respond to the resulting movement.
The sensory pathway carries information to the brain. Becoming aware of the tone is sensation.
Recognizing the tone as a notification is perception. The brain gives meaning to the information.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Follow a different sense
guided.instruction: Sunlight warms your skin. Complete the explanation.

items.prompt: Which receptor category detects the temperature change?
items.hint: Name what changes at the skin.
items.explanation: Thermoreceptors detect temperature change. The light source is not the same thing as the stimulus detected in this skin example.

items.prompt: You become aware that your skin feels warm. Which term fits this conscious experience?
items.hint: Distinguish detection at a receptor from awareness in the brain.
items.explanation: Sensation is becoming aware of the input. Reception began when the receptors detected the change.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Light getting in is only one step
worked.scenario: An eye has a clear cornea and lens, but its photoreceptors are damaged.
steps: The clear cornea and lens may still allow light through and focus it on the retina.
The retina contains rods and cones. Damaged receptors may not convert the light into normal signals.
Light must reach the retina, but that alone does not produce vision. The receptors and the pathway carrying their information must also work.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Complete the light route
guided.instruction: Use the sequence cornea → aqueous humour → pupil → lens → vitreous humour → retina.

items.prompt: Which structure changes the size of the opening in that route?
items.hint: The pupil is an opening within a ring of muscle.
items.explanation: Iris muscles change pupil size and control how much light enters.

items.prompt: Which part contains the receptors that detect the light?
items.hint: Clear materials let light pass; receptors detect it.
items.explanation: Rods and cones are in the retina. The humours transmit light and the sclera protects the eye.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Looking from far away to nearby
worked.scenario: You stop looking at a distant clock and look down at a book.
steps: Near vision needs stronger bending of incoming light.
The ciliary muscle contracts, reducing the pull of the suspensory ligaments.
The lens becomes rounder. Its stronger focusing effect helps form a clear image on the retina.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Now reverse the change
guided.instruction: You look from the book back to the distant clock.

items.prompt: The ciliary muscle relaxes. What happens to ligament tension?
items.hint: A distant object needs a flatter lens.
items.explanation: Relaxation allows the suspensory ligaments to become more taut.

items.answer: The lens flattens and bends light less strongly
options: The lens flattens and bends light less strongly
The lens rounds and bends light more strongly
items.explanation: Greater ligament tension stretches the lens flatter, reducing its focusing power for distant vision.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Separate incoming light from outgoing information
steps: Incoming light passes the ganglion-cell layer, then the bipolar-cell layer, before reaching rods and cones.
Rods and cones detect the light and change their signalling. Information passes to bipolar cells and then ganglion cells.
Ganglion-cell axons form the optic nerve. This route carries neural information, not light.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Fill the two routes
guided.instruction: Choose the missing stage in each route.

items.prompt: Incoming light: ganglion-cell layer → ____ → rods and cones.
items.hint: Think about the middle retinal layer.
items.explanation: Light passes through the bipolar-cell layer before reaching the photoreceptors.

items.prompt: Neural information: rods and cones → bipolar cells → ____ → optic nerve.
items.hint: Which cells send their axons into the optic nerve?
items.explanation: Ganglion cells receive information from the retinal circuit, and their axons form the optic nerve.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Locate the first affected step
worked.scenario: Fluid in the middle ear reduces how well the eardrum and ossicles move.
steps: The problem affects mechanical transmission before the receptors.
Less vibration can reach the oval window and cochlear fluid.
Hair-cell stimulation may be reduced even if the hair cells and auditory nerve are not damaged.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Movement becomes neural information
guided.instruction: Follow the energy through the hearing pathway.

items.prompt: Immediately after the stapes moves the oval window, what happens?
items.answer: Pressure waves move through cochlear fluid
options: The auditory nerve carries sound waves
Pressure waves move through cochlear fluid
items.explanation: Oval-window movement creates fluid pressure waves in the cochlea.

items.prompt: Which event performs the sensory conversion?
items.answer: Bending of hair-cell projections changes cell signalling
options: Bending of hair-cell projections changes cell signalling
items.hint: Choose the receptor event rather than a supporting structure.
items.explanation: Hair cells transduce movement into changed electrical and chemical signalling, which affects auditory nerve fibres.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Separate a louder note from a higher note
worked.scenario: A recorded tone becomes louder while its frequency stays constant.
steps: Frequency has not changed, so its pitch stays approximately the same.
The larger pressure variation means the wave amplitude has increased.
The nervous system represents the stronger input through activity patterns, not taller individual action potentials.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Compare two described waves
guided.instruction: These are invented comparison values, not a hearing test: A has 4 cycles in 0.01 s; B has 8 cycles in 0.01 s. They have equal amplitudes.

items.prompt: Which sound has the higher pitch?
options: They must have the same pitch
items.hint: Compare cycle counts over the same time.
items.explanation: B has more cycles in the same interval, so its frequency and expected pitch are higher.

items.prompt: What does equal amplitude support in this simplified comparison?
options: B must be twice as loud
items.hint: Amplitude and frequency describe different wave properties.
items.explanation: Equal amplitudes support a similar-loudness comparison here. The cycle counts still differ, so pitch differs.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Classify straight-line acceleration
worked.scenario: An elevator starts moving upward while a passenger keeps their head facing forward.
steps: The described change is vertical straight-line acceleration, not head rotation.
The saccule is especially relevant. Acceleration shifts its weighted otolithic membrane relative to hair cells.
Bending the hair-cell projections changes signalling about the movement.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Compare turning with moving straight
guided.instruction: Use the structure that matches each kind of movement.

items.prompt: Your head starts turning to look over your shoulder. Which mechanism fits?
items.answer: Fluid movement bends a cupula in a semicircular canal
options: A weighted membrane in the saccule detects a sound wave
Fluid movement bends a cupula in a semicircular canal
items.explanation: Relative fluid movement in a semicircular canal bends the cupula and hair-cell projections.

items.prompt: A vehicle starts moving straight forward. Which structure is especially relevant?
items.hint: Horizontal acceleration differs from a turn.
items.explanation: The utricle helps detect horizontal linear acceleration through movement of its weighted otolithic membrane.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Model a complete investigation plan
worked.scenario: Plan only: compare touch discrimination on a fingertip and the forearm. Do not perform the test.
steps: Question: Does the smallest separation reported as two contacts differ between these body regions?
Prediction: The fingertip will distinguish closer contacts because its sensory representation is generally more precise.
Manipulated variable: body region. Responding variable: the smallest separation reported as two contacts, measured in millimetres.
Controls: use the same contact method, pressure, contact duration and instructions. Plan repeated trials with the same participant and more than one participant before making broad conclusions.
Safety and evidence: this is a written plan only. No physical testing or sharp objects are required. A completed data table would need real observations; a prediction is not a result.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Complete part of a second plan
guided.instruction: A written plan compares the palm with the forearm. The question concerns the smallest separation reported as two contacts.

items.hint: Identify what the plan deliberately changes.
items.explanation: The plan changes which body region is considered. The smallest reported separation is the measured response.

items.prompt: The plan changes both body region and contact pressure. What needs fixing?
items.answer: Keep pressure consistent so the region comparison is fair
options: Keep pressure consistent so the region comparison is fair
Record the prediction as the result
items.hint: More than one changing factor makes the result harder to explain.
items.explanation: Keeping pressure consistent helps isolate the effect of body region. Repeated trials can then help assess consistency.
